# Zeros of Bessel Functions
SciencePedia SciencePedia

Definition

Zeros of Bessel Functions is a mathematical concept representing the discrete values where Bessel functions equal zero, serving as the allowed solutions for wave phenomena in systems with circular boundaries. These zeros are fundamental to the fields of acoustics and physics, where they determine the vibrational frequencies of drumheads and the quantized energy levels of confined quantum particles. The zeros exhibit an interlacing property between consecutive orders and their spacing approaches the constant value π at infinity, providing critical cutoff conditions for light modes in optical fibers.

## Abstract

In this work, we investigate the loss factor of axisymmetric and rectangular tapered collimators over a broad range of bunch lengths and geometrical parameters using the electromagnetic simulation codes ECHO and GdfidL. The calculations are performed for Gaussian bunches of rms length $\sigma_{s}$, with the collimator geometry characterized by the minimum and maximum apertures $b$ and $d$, taper length $L$, and chamber width $W$ for rectangular structures. For short bunches and tapered collimators with $d-b>b$, we extend the phenomenological formula previously obtained for axisymmetric to rectangular tapered collimators, describing the dependence of the loss factor on bunch length and taper geometry through an arctangent function of the scaling parameter $\mu d^{2}/(\sigma_{s}L)$. We demonstrate that this parameter is related to a Fresnel number and, by combining diffraction theory with the electrodynamics of the beam-induced image charge, analytically explain the factor of two between the coefficients $\mu=0.2$ and $\mu=0.4$ for axisymmetric and rectangular collimators, respectively. The resulting expression is applicable to rectangular collimators with $W/(2d)\geq 1.8$, extending its validity beyond the idealized flat geometry. For longer bunches, we identify the transition from the optical to the inductive regime and derive an analytical expression for the loss factor based on the cutoff wavenumber of the lowest relevant electromagnetic mode.

Any solution of Bessel's differential equation falls under this umbrella name, which collectively covers the Bessel function of the first kind J n (x), the Neumann (second kind) function Y n (x), and the complex Hankel function combinations. ###### Abstract

In this work, we investigate the loss factor of axisymmetric and rectangular tapered collimators over a broad range of bunch lengths and geometrical parameters using the electromagnetic simulation codes ECHO and GdfidL. The calculations are performed for Gaussian bunches of rms length \sigma_{s}, with the collimator geometry characterized by the minimum and maximum apertures b and d, taper length L, and chamber width W for rectangular structures. For short bunches and tapered collimators with d-b>b, we extend the phenomenological formula previously obtained for axisymmetric to rectangular tapered collimators, describing the dependence of the loss factor on bunch length and taper geometry through an arctangent function of the scaling parameter \mu d^{2}/(\sigma_{s}L). We demonstrate that this parameter is related to a Fresnel number and, by combining diffraction theory with the electrodynamics of the beam-induced image charge, analytically explain the factor of two between the coefficients \mu=0.2 and \mu=0.4 for axisymmetric and rectangular collimators, respectively. The resulting expression is applicable to rectangular collimators with W/(2d)\geq 1.8, extending its validity beyond the idealized flat geometry. For longer bunches, we identify the transition from the optical to the inductive regime and derive an analytical expression for the loss factor based on the cutoff wavenumber of the lowest relevant electromagnetic mode.

In single photon emission computed tomography, the choice of the collimator has a major impact on the sensitivity and resolution of the system. Traditional parallel-hole and fan-beam collimators used in clinical practice, for example, have a relatively poor sensitivity and subcentimeter spatial resolution, while in small-animal imaging, pinhole collimators are used to obtain submillimeter resolution and multiple pinholes are often combined to increase sensitivity. This paper reviews methods for production, sensitivity maximization, and task-based optimization of collimation for both clinical and preclinical imaging applications. New opportunities for improved collimation are now arising primarily because of (i) new collimator-production techniques and (ii) detectors with improved intrinsic spatial resolution that have recently become available. $$

 where $\alpha$ is a number that determines the shape of the solution. This number is called the _order_ of the Bessel function and can be any complex number. Although the same equation arises for both $\alpha$ and $- \alpha$, mathematicians define separate Bessel functions for each to ensure the functions behave smoothly as the order changes.

## What waveguide cutoff frequency is  
A waveguide is a hollow metal pipe that carries electromagnetic waves, and every propagation mode in that pipe has a **cutoff frequency**: the lowest frequency at which the mode can carry power. Above its cutoff, a mode propagates with a guide wavelength longer than the free-space wavelength. Below its cutoff, the mode is **evanescent**: the fields decay exponentially along the guide instead of traveling. Nothing about the length of the pipe or the power of the source changes this threshold. It is set entirely by the cross-section geometry - the width and height of a rectangular guide, the radius of a circular one - plus the dielectric filling and the mode indices.  
Cutoff is why waveguide systems are specified in bands. A designer picks a guide whose dominant-mode cutoff sits comfortably below the lowest operating frequency, while keeping the next higher-order mode's cutoff above the highest operating frequency. That window is the single-mode band: only one field pattern can propagate, so the signal cannot hop into a different mode at a bend or flange and corrupt the measurement. The third tab of this calculator tests exactly this condition for any frequency and cutoff pair, and reports the guide wavelength when the verdict is propagating.
## Circular waveguide cutoff and the Bessel roots  
Circular guides replace the sine/cosine mode indices with **Bessel functions**, and the cutoff formula becomes:  
c= χ · c / (2πR)  
Here R is the inside radius and χ is a root that depends on the mode. TEmn modes use χ′mn, the zeros of the derivative of the m-th Bessel function; TMmn modes use χmn, the zeros of the Bessel function itself. These numbers are fixed mathematical constants, not fit parameters:

Bessel functions J_n and Y_n solve x²y'' + xy' + (x² − n²)y = 0. They describe vibrating drumhead modes, cylindrical waveguides, and FM radio sidebands.
Cutoff frequencies are set by zeros of J_m or J_m'. Heat flow in cylinders. Cooling of rods, heating of pipes, thermal time constant R²/(α₁² κ) using the first zero of J_0. Title: Loss Factor of Axisymmetric and Rectangular Tapered Collimators from Optical to Inductive Regimes

Authors: Md Wahidur Rahman (1), Alexei Blednykh (1), Gang Wang (1), Xiaofeng Gu (1) ((1) Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, New York, USA)

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: In this work, we investigate the loss factor of axisymmetric and rectangular tapered collimators over a broad range of bunch lengths and geometrical parameters using the electromagnetic simulation codes ECHO and GdfidL. The calculations are performed for Gaussian bunches of rms length $\sigma_s$ , with the collimator geometry characterized by the minimum and maximum apertures $b$ and $d$ , taper length $L$ , and chamber width $W$ for rectangular structures. For short bunches and tapered collimators with $d-b>b$ , we extend the phenomenological formula previously obtained for axisymmetric to rectangular tapered collimators, describing the dependence of the loss factor on bunch length and taper geometry through an arctangent function of the scaling parameter $\mu d^2/(\sigma_s L)$ . We demonstrate that this parameter is related to a Fresnel number and, by combining diffraction theory with the electrodynamics of the beam-induced image charge, analytically explain the factor of two between the coefficients $\mu=0.2$ and $\mu=0.4$ for axisymmetric and rectangular collimators, respectively. The resulting expression is applicable to rectangular collimators with $W/(2d) \geq 1.8$ , extending its validity beyond the idealized flat geometry. For longer bunches, we identify the transition from the optical to the inductive regime and derive an analytical expression for the loss factor based on the cutoff wavenumber of the lowest relevant electromagnetic mode.

octen.snippet: The longitudinal distributions of the maximum intensity in Bessel light beams (BLBs) of various orders are compared with analogous distributions in Gaussian and Laguerre-Gaussian light beams of the corresponding orders. The concept of a “dangerous zone” of the BLB is introduced. A method for determining its length is proposed. The maximum intensity I0 of the initial Gaussian or Laguerre-Gaussian light beam is initially chosen not to exceed the optical damage threshold of the optical elements and objects used. The dangerous zone of the BLB is the region of space behind the axicon in which the maximum intensity in the BLB exceeds I0. The length of the dangerous zone is taken to be the largest distance zK behind the axicon for which the maximum intensity in the BLB cross section is equal to I0. Additionally, the distance zE from the axicon at which the intensity on the BLB axis and in its peripheral annular field are aligned is determined. The maximum intensity in this cross section in BLBs of the 0th, 1st, and 2nd orders are guaranteed to be less than I0 although the transverse size of the light beam is not yet too large. The relative (in units of the BLB existence length zwI) values of zE and zK for the zero and higher (from the 1st to the 9th) orders of the BLB are calculated with the help of mathematical modeling methods. It is advisable to place objects with low optical damage thresholds at distances greater than zK when designing optical systems using the conical BLB geometry.

Abstract
We propose and experimentally demonstrate a novel experimental scheme to generate high on-axis peak intensity, segmented, smooth, zero-order quasi-Bessel beams with tunable ranges. Illuminating the axicon with hollow Gaussian beams (HGBs) of different orders, we have generated Bessel beams of varying ranges at different positions away from the axicon. The presence of a dark core at the center of the HGBs removes the effect of imperfection in the axicon tip. As a result, the entire power of the input beam is transformed into a zero-order Bessel beam without any on-axis intensity modulation. We observe the decrease in range and increase in on-axis peak intensity of the zero-order Bessel beam with the order of HGBs. Controlling the superposition of the HGBs of different orders to the axicon, we have demonstrated the increase in the range of the Bessel beam. The current technique can also produce Bessel beams of different intensity distributions, including single-peak or multiple-peak Bessel beams. Using single-pass second-harmonic generation in nonlinear crystals of different lengths, we have further verified the increase of on-axis peak intensity of the Bessel beam with the order of the HGBs and the increase in the range of the Bessel beam due to the superposed HGBs.

parallel-fast.title: Loss Factor of Axisymmetric and Rectangular Tapered Collimators from Optical to Inductive Regimes
parallel-fast.snippet:
In this work, we investigate the loss factor of axisymmetric and rectangular tapered collimators over a broad range of bunch lengths and geometrical parameters using the electromagnetic simulation codes ECHO and GdfidL. The calculations are performed for Gaussian bunches of rms length $\sigma_{s}$ , with the collimator geometry characterized by the minimum and maximum apertures $b$ and $d$ , taper length $L$ , and chamber width $W$ for rectangular structures. For short bunches and tapered collimators with $d-b>b$ , we extend the phenomenological formula previously obtained for axisymmetric to rectangular tapered collimators, describing the dependence of the loss factor on bunch length and taper geometry through an arctangent function of the scaling parameter $\mu d^{2}/(\sigma_{s}L)$ . We demonstrate that this parameter is related to a Fresnel number and, by combining diffraction theory with the electrodynamics of the beam-induced image charge, analytically explain the factor of two between the coefficients $\mu=0.2$ and $\mu=0.4$ for axisymmetric and rectangular collimators, respectively. The resulting expression is applicable to rectangular collimators with $W/(2d)\geq 1.8$ , extending its validity beyond the idealized flat geometry. For longer bunches, we identify the transition from the optical to the inductive regime and derive an analytical expression for the loss factor based on the cutoff wavenumber of the lowest relevant electromagnetic mode.

Any solution of Bessel's differential equation falls under this umbrella name, which collectively covers the Bessel function of the first kind Jn(x), the Neumann (second kind) function Yn(x), and the complex Hankel function combinations. These functions describe how a field varies with radius in cylindrical coordinates, which is exactly the geometry of a circular waveguide, a coaxial line, or a current filament radiating cylindrical waves. The zeros of Jn and its derivative set the eigenvalues pnm = Jn root and p′nm = Jn′ root that fix every TM and TE cutoff frequency, with the dominant TE11 mode tied to p′11 = 1.841 and the lowest TM mode TM01 tied to p01 = 2.405.

## Why Cylindrical Geometry Demands Bessel Solutions

When the Helmholtz wave equation is separated in cylindrical coordinates (ρ, φ, z), the angular part yields harmonic functions ejnφ with integer order n, the axial part yields traveling waves e−jβz, and the radial part collapses to Bessel's equation. The radial solutions are the cylinder functions. This is the cylindrical analog of using sines and cosines in rectangular problems or Legendre functions in spherical problems. Because Bessel's equation is second order, it always has two linearly independent solutions: Jn(x), which is finite and oscillatory at the origin, and Yn(x), which diverges logarithmically (n = 0) or as a negative power (n ≥ 1) as the argument approaches zero.

The physics of the region picks which combination survives. Inside a solid air-filled circular guide the field must remain finite on the axis, so only Jn is admissible and Yn is discarded. In a coaxial structure the inner conductor removes the axis from the field region, so both Jn and Yn are retained and combined to satisfy the conditions at both conductor radii. Bessel functions are the standard solutions of x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − n²)y = 0, the equation that appears whenever a wave, vibration, or diffusion problem has cylindrical symmetry: a vibrating drumhead, heat spreading along a rod, microwaves in a circular waveguide, light diffracting through a round aperture. ## Introduction to waveguide cutoff and modal propagation

Waveguide cutoff is the frequency boundary at which a particular electromagnetic field pattern changes from decaying along a metal guide to propagating through it. Unlike coaxial cable, a hollow conducting waveguide does not support a TEM mode. Its walls force the fields into discrete transverse patterns called modes. Each mode has a family, TE or TM, and indices that describe its transverse variation. Below that mode’s cutoff, the axial field is evanescent; above it, the mode can carry power.

This calculator evaluates ideal rectangular and circular guides. It finds the selected TE or TM cutoff, identifies low-order modes, and, when an operating frequency is supplied, estimates guide wavelength, phase velocity, group velocity, or below-cutoff decay. Cutoff is a boundary-condition result rather than a complete component rating. Launches, flanges, bends, windows, surface finish, material loss, and tolerance all affect a finished assembly.
